scenes.animation: A prison cell on an island, labelled 'Robben Island'. A tally of scratches on the wall counts up to '28 years'. The cell door opens and an older man walks out into sunlight as crowds cheer. A caption: 'Nelson Mandela'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Twenty-eight years in prison? What did he do?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He fought against a system called apartheid. His story explains why countries need constitutions.

scenes.animation: A courtroom scene in sepia: 'Treason trial, 1964'. Nelson Mandela and seven other leaders stand before a judge; the gavel falls: 'Life imprisonment'. A boat carries them to Robben Island.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Nelson Mandela and seven other leaders were sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964, for daring to oppose the apartheid regime in South Africa.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He spent the next 28 years in South Africa's most dreaded prison, Robben Island.

scenes.animation: A split town scene: separate trains, buses, hospitals, schools, beaches and even churches, each with signboards 'Whites only' and 'Blacks'. Colour-coded people are pushed to different sides. A title card: 'Apartheid = racial discrimination'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Apartheid was the name of a system of racial discrimination unique to South Africa. It was imposed by the white Europeans.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The system divided people and labelled them on the basis of their skin colour. The blacks, who were about three-fourth of the population, were called natives. They were forbidden from living in white areas, and did not have voting rights.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Trains, buses, taxis, hotels, hospitals, schools, beaches and even churches were separate for whites and blacks.

scenes.animation: Protest marches fill the streets with banners of the 'African National Congress'. Workers' unions, churches and some white supporters join in. The government sends police, and the struggle continues across years on a scrolling timeline.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Did people just accept this?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. Since 1950, the blacks, coloured people and Indians fought against apartheid. They launched protest marches and strikes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The African National Congress was the umbrella organisation that led the struggle. Many workers' unions and the Communist Party joined it. Many sensitive whites also joined the ANC and played a leading role.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The racist government continued to rule by detaining, torturing and killing thousands of black and coloured people.

scenes.animation: A 'BOARD TIP' card: 'Apartheid — South Africa | Mandela jailed 1964 | 28 years in Robben Island | ANC led the struggle'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: short questions often ask what apartheid was, and which organisation led the struggle against it. The answer is the African National Congress.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a broken chain icon. Points appear: '1. Mandela and 7 others jailed for life in 1964; 28 years in Robben Island', '2. Apartheid: racial discrimination imposed by white Europeans', '3. ANC led the struggle with protests and strikes'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Nelson Mandela was jailed in 1964 and spent 28 years on Robben Island.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: apartheid was a system of racial discrimination imposed by the white Europeans in South Africa.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the African National Congress led the long struggle against it.

name: A New Constitution for South Africa and Why We Need One

scenes.animation: Midnight, 26 April 1994. An old flag is lowered and a colourful new South African flag rises. Fireworks burst; people of all colours dance together. Zippy waves two tiny flags.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A new flag at midnight! What happened?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: South Africa became a democracy. And it needed a brand new rulebook.

scenes.animation: A timeline: 'Protests grow' → 'Discriminatory laws repealed' → 'Ban on political parties and media lifted' → 'Mandela released after 28 years' → '26 April 1994: new flag, democratic republic' → 'Mandela becomes first President'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: As protests grew, the white regime realised it could no longer keep the blacks under its rule through repression. Discriminatory laws were repealed, and the ban on political parties and restrictions on the media were lifted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After 28 years of imprisonment, Nelson Mandela walked out of jail as a free man.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: At the midnight of 26 April 1994, the new national flag of the Republic of South Africa was unfurled. Mandela became the first President of this new South Africa.

scenes.animation: Two groups sit at a round table: one group holds a card 'Majority rule, social and economic rights', the other 'Protect our property and privileges'. They slowly push their cards together into one document: 'Constitution — one of the finest in the world'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The black majority wanted to make sure that democratic majority rule was not compromised, and wanted substantial social and economic rights. The white minority wanted to protect its privileges and property.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After two years of discussion, they agreed. Nobody should be excluded, and no one should be treated as a demon. Everyone should become part of the solution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The result was a constitution that gave its citizens the most extensive rights available in any country. It is often called one of the finest constitutions the world has.

scenes.animation: A flowchart builds from a book labelled 'Constitution': four arrows lead to 'Generates trust and coordination', 'Specifies how government is constituted', 'Lays down limits on the powers of government', 'Expresses aspirations of the people'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why do countries even need a constitution? Can't they just be nice?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A constitution is a set of written rules accepted by all people living together in a country. It is the supreme law.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: First, it generates a degree of trust and coordination among different kinds of people. Second, it specifies how the government will be constituted and who will take which decisions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Third, it lays down limits on the powers of the government and tells us the rights of citizens. Fourth, it expresses the aspirations of the people about creating a good society.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: these four functions of a constitution make a classic four-mark answer.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a rolled constitution icon. Points appear: '1. 26 April 1994: South Africa became a democracy; Mandela first President', '2. Blacks and whites agreed on one of the finest constitutions', '3. A constitution builds trust, sets up government, limits power, expresses aspirations'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: on 26 April 1994, South Africa became a democracy with Mandela as its first President.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the oppressors and the oppressed agreed on one of the finest constitutions in the world.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a constitution builds trust, sets up the government, limits its powers and expresses people's aspirations.

scenes.animation: A giant book lands on Zippy's desk with a thud: 'Constitution of India'. He tries to lift it and wobbles. Behind him, a hall full of people in 1940s clothes are debating, papers flying.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Who wrote this massive book, and how long did it take?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hundreds of people, over three years, in very difficult times. Let's go back.

scenes.animation: A difficult-times montage: partition maps being split, refugee trains, princely state crowns scattered on a map. Label: 'Birth of a nation amid partition and violence'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: India's Constitution was drawn up under very difficult circumstances. The country was born through a partition on the basis of religious differences, which saw large-scale violence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The British had also left it to the rulers of the princely states to decide whether to merge with India, with Pakistan or remain independent.

scenes.animation: A timeline stretches across the screen: '1928 — Motilal Nehru and eight other Congress leaders draft a constitution for India', '1931 — Karachi session resolution on what independent India's constitution should look like'. Small icons show 'universal adult franchise', 'right to freedom and equality'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yet the makers were not starting from scratch. In 1928, Motilal Nehru and eight other Congress leaders drafted a constitution for India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1931, the resolution at the Karachi session of the Indian National Congress dwelt on how independent India's constitution should look like.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Both committed to universal adult franchise, the right to freedom and equality, and protecting the rights of minorities.

scenes.animation: A grand hall fills with members; a counter shows '299 members'. Date stamps: 'Elections: July 1946', 'First meeting: December 1946', 'Adopted: 26 November 1949', 'Came into effect: 26 January 1950'. Dr B.R. Ambedkar sits at the head of a table labelled 'Drafting Committee — Chairman'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The drafting of the document was done by an assembly of elected representatives called the Constituent Assembly. Elections to it were held in July 1946, and its first meeting was held in December 1946.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After partition, the Assembly was divided. The Constituent Assembly that wrote the Indian constitution had 299 members.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into effect on 26 January 1950. That's why we celebrate 26 January as Republic Day.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar. The Assembly discussed the draft clause by clause, and considered more than two thousand amendments.

scenes.animation: Zippy writes '26 January 1950 — adopted' on a board. A buzzer sounds and a 'BOARD TIP' card corrects it: '26 Nov 1949 = adopted (Constitution Day) | 26 Jan 1950 = came into effect (Republic Day)'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So it was adopted on 26 January 1950?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, it came into effect then. It was adopted on 26 November 1949. Board tip: mixing up these two dates is the most common mistake in this chapter.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a book and a calendar icon. Points appear: '1. Made amid partition and violence; built on 1928 draft and 1931 Karachi resolution', '2. Constituent Assembly: 299 members; Drafting Committee chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar', '3. Adopted 26 Nov 1949; in effect 26 Jan 1950'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: our Constitution was made in difficult times, building on the 1928 draft and the 1931 Karachi resolution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the Constituent Assembly had 299 members, and Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: it was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950.

name: The Preamble: Guiding Values of the Constitution

scenes.animation: A school morning assembly. A student reads a scroll aloud: 'We, the people of India...'. Zippy yawns in the front row, then perks up when Neo whispers that it's the most important paragraph of the Constitution.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: We read this every week. Is it really that important?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It's the Preamble. It contains the philosophy on which the whole Constitution is built.

scenes.animation: The Preamble scroll unrolls. Key words light up one by one as floating tiles: 'We, the people of India', 'Sovereign', 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Democratic', 'Republic'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Preamble begins with 'We, the people of India'. This means the Constitution has been drawn up and enacted by the people through their representatives, and not handed down by a king or an outside power.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sovereign means people have supreme right to make decisions on internal as well as external matters. Socialist means wealth is generated socially and should be shared equally by society.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Secular means citizens have complete freedom to follow any religion, and there is no official religion. Democratic means people enjoy equal political rights, elect their rulers and hold them accountable.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Republic means the head of the state is an elected person, and not a hereditary position.

scenes.animation: Four more tiles light up and form a square: 'Justice', 'Liberty', 'Equality', 'Fraternity'. Small scenes play inside each: a fair judge, a bird leaving a cage, two kids on a level see-saw, and friends holding hands.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Justice means citizens cannot be discriminated against on the grounds of caste, religion and gender, and social inequalities have to be reduced.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Liberty means there are no unreasonable restrictions on what citizens think, how they wish to express their thoughts, and the way they wish to follow up their thoughts in action.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Equality means all are equal before the law. Fraternity means all of us should behave as if we are members of the same family. No one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior.

scenes.animation: Zippy tries to match 'Republic' with a king's crown and gets a red cross. A 'BOARD TIP' card: 'Republic = elected head of state, not hereditary'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Republic means a strong king, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The opposite! Our head of state, the President, is elected. Board tip: meanings of Preamble words are asked every year, so learn each one in a single line.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the Preamble scroll. Points appear: '1. We, the people of India: the Constitution comes from the people', '2. Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic', '3. Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: 'We, the people of India' shows that the Constitution comes from the people.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: India is a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: it promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity to all citizens.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Okay, next assembly, I'm reading it the loudest.
